transcript.text: Good morning, everyone. Thank you for being here. As you know, the eighth-grade civics class has proposed an oral-history project in which 20 student interviewers would record interviews with community members about local history using their personal phones, with all recordings published on the public school website and retained indefinitely. Before I can sign off on this, I need to hear findings from each of you — the project advisor, the counselor, and the instructional technology coordinator. Let's work through this together so we can determine whether this project is ready for approval.
transcript.speaker: A1

transcript.text: Dr. Morgan, as project advisor, my roster review shows that exactly eight students have completed the district's media-ethics training: J1, J3, J6, J8, J11, J14, J17, and J20. Only those eight may conduct recorded interviews, and the approval file must include a training-verification record. So the plan as drafted — calling for 20 student interviewers — would need to be revised to limit recorded interviews to these eight trained students.
transcript.speaker: A2

transcript.text: Dr. Morgan, my family-consent review reveals a significant issue. Five of the proposed interviewees — I2, I5, I9, I14, and I18 — have not granted permission for public web publication. Their recordings may be used only in the school's internal archive, and the plan must include a consent-exclusion record. This means the draft plan's call to publish ALL recordings on the public school website would need to be revised to exclude these five interviewees' recordings from public publication.
transcript.speaker: A3

transcript.text: Dr. Morgan, my technology review confirms that personal phones cannot be used for school recordings. The project must use district tablets instead, and source files must be stored in the restricted OralHistory drive. Recordings must be deleted exactly 45 days after the final class presentation. Storing source files in that restricted drive does not prohibit publishing consented recordings on the public school website, so Mr. Lewis's consent exclusions can still be honored. Additionally, the technology plan must include a secure-storage configuration record. This means the draft plan's call for personal phone recording and indefinite retention would both need to be revised.
